strengths: Practical and clearly motivated contribution: the paper directly targets the well-documented efficiency-fidelity gap of neural-motion-field dynamic 3DGS (DeformableGS/4DGS), and the three modules (TSP, TSS, GroupFlow) are complementary and well-integrated into a unified pipeline.

Very comprehensive empirical evaluation: results span MonoDyGauBench (50 scenes across 5 datasets), NeRF-DS, D-NeRF, HyperNeRF, and iPhone, with experiments repeated three times and averaged, plus per-scene results in the appendix (Tables 11-15).

Thorough ablation studies: sweeps over soft/hard pruning percentages (Figure 5), group count J (Table 10), and cumulative module combinations (Tables 1, 8, 9) give good insight into design choices; the claim that pruning suppresses noise that hinders motion grouping is supported by the J-ablation.

Results are reported honestly: quality drops under aggressive settings are visible in the tables (e.g., 4DGS+Pruning PSNR 23.55→22.44; D-NeRF full pipeline PSNR 35.07 vs 38.92 baseline) and are acknowledged in the Limitations section rather than hidden.

The core technical ideas are reasonable and well formalized: the temporal sensitivity score (Eq. 5-6) is a sensible extension of Hessian/gradient-based pruning to dynamic settings, and the timestamp perturbation in TSS (Eq. 7) is a lightweight mechanism for exposing temporally unstable Gaussians.

Large, well-documented speedups: e.g., 10.68x rendering and 2.44x training acceleration on NeRF-DS with essentially neutral PSNR/SSIM (Table 1), and 29.21x rendering on HyperNeRF, with pruning also enabling training within 24GB VRAM where baselines OOM.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: TSP is a fairly direct adaptation of gradient/Hessian-based pruning (PUP-3DGS, Speedy-Splat) to the dynamic setting with a temporal aggregation, and GroupFlow is closely related to existing grouped/rigid motion methods (SC-GS, DynMF, RigsGS); the paper positions this as generalization but the delta over prior art is incremental.

TSS is a thin contribution: a Gaussian-noise annealing schedule on timestamps is a simple regularizer, and the evidence for its benefit is mostly small SSIM/PSNR deltas (e.g., +0.002-0.003 on NeRF-DS) plus qualitative claims about floater suppression.

GroupFlow involves a clear fidelity trade-off when used alone: on NeRF-DS PSNR drops 23.80→23.54, on 4DGS it drops 23.55→21.00, and on D-NeRF the full pipeline loses ~3.8 dB versus the baseline; the paper's headline of 'preserving neural-field fidelity' only holds for the pruning variants on some datasets.

GroupFlow adds model size rather than reducing it in some settings (e.g., HyperNeRF size grows from 159.30MB to 179.79MB with GroupFlow, Table 9; the 1.94MB deformation network claim applies only after pruning), which complicates the efficiency narrative.

Comparisons are restricted to two backbones (DeformableGS, 4DGS) within MonoDyGauBench; there is no head-to-head against other recent efficient dynamic 3DGS compression/pruning methods (e.g., Mega, Temporally-compressed 3DGS, LGS) that target the same efficiency goal.

Several hyperparameters (lambda_r=0.5 'empirically selected', Nsamp=100, beta=0.1, tau=20000, J=2048) are justified only post-hoc via ablations on two datasets; generalization of these choices across the 50-scene benchmark is asserted but not individually validated.

Some presentation inconsistencies: Figure 1/abstract emphasize 9.88x/11.37x on a single HyperNeRF scene (chicken), while the aggregate numbers are more modest; FPS results from the standalone codebase vs the MonoDyGauBench wrapper differ (Appendix A.6), making cross-figure FPS comparisons confusing.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the method is tested across NeRF-DS, D-NeRF, HyperNeRF, Nerfies, iPhone, and the 50-scene MonoDyGauBench, with results averaged over three runs, per-scene breakdowns, and ablations over soft/hard pruning ratios and group counts (Appendix A.3/A.4, Figure 5).

The efficiency gains are large and consistently reported: 6.78x rendering and 2.18x training speedup over DeformableGS on MonoDyGauBench, growing to 13.71x / 2.53x with GroupFlow, and up to 29.21x on HyperNeRF, with ~10-12x fewer Gaussians.

The modules are positioned as general-purpose: TSP/TSS can in principle be attached to any dynamic 3DGS framework with an explicit motion field, which increases the paper's potential usefulness beyond the specific DeformableGS instantiation.

The paper is generally well written and honest about trade-offs, e.g., Section 6 acknowledges fidelity loss under extreme pruning and reduced fidelity for highly non-rigid regions, and Table 2 visibly shows quality drops for GroupFlow on 4DGS.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. All three components are natural extensions of existing work: TSP is a temporal generalization of gradient/Hessian sensitivity pruning from static 3DGS (PUP-3DGS, Speedy-Splat, explicitly acknowledged); TSS is a small timestamp-perturbation trick; and distilling neural motion into grouped rigid transforms is well explored in SC-GS, DynMF, RiTGS, and SPGaussian. The paper reads more as a careful engineering integration of these ideas than a new insight.

Comparison breadth is insufficient for the efficiency claims. The evaluation is largely self-referential (the method applied to two baselines it chose), plus the MonoDyGauBench table. There is no comparison against existing efficient/compressed dynamic 3DGS methods such as MEGA, Swift4D, EAGLES, TeCC, or LGS, which directly target the same speed-fidelity trade-off; 'over 100 FPS faster than the fastest baseline' is claimed only relative to the benchmark's five formulations.

The fidelity claims are overstated in places. In Table 2 the full pipeline has worse LPIPS than the baseline DeformableGS (0.313 vs 0.283 on MonoDyGauBench) and on D-NeRF (Table 8: 0.0365 vs 0.0143, PSNR 35.07 vs 36.92); applied to 4DGS, GroupFlow degrades PSNR from 23.55 to 21.00. The abstract's claim of 'surpassing all non-neural methods in speed while outperforming every non-neural method in image quality' does not hold uniformly (e.g., RTGS has better PSNR than the 4DGS+GroupFlow variant).

GroupFlow results are inconsistent across settings: on HyperNeRF it alone increases model size (179.79 MB vs 159.30 MB baseline in Table 9) and the paper itself reports that GroupFlow slightly hurts D-NeRF PSNR and training speed within MonoDyGauBench (Appendix A.1). The 'mild regularizing effect' explanation is asserted but not mechanistically analyzed.

Several important design choices are empirically fixed rather than justified: J=2048 groups, Nsamp=100, the 60%/30% soft/hard pruning schedule, and lambda_r=0.5. The ablations show these matter, but there is little guidance or analysis for transfer to new scenes/methods, which weakens reproducibility in practice.

The rendering speedups partially conflate sources: FPS gains come from fewer primitives, removal of per-Gaussian MLP inference, and batching of SE(3) transforms, but the paper does not decompose how much each contributes, making it hard to judge which component is genuinely novel versus borrowed speed from prior pruning work.
No code or release statement is provided in the manuscript, which limits reproducibility for a systems/efficiency paper whose value depends on practical adoption.

strengths: Practical and well-motivated contribution: bridging the efficiency–fidelity gap of neural-motion-field dynamic 3DGS is a real problem, and the proposed SpeeDe3DGS pipeline delivers large, consistently measured speedups (6.78×–13.71× rendering, 2.18×–2.53× training on MonoDyGauBench; up to 29.21× on HyperNeRF) with only mild fidelity loss.

Comprehensive and careful empirical support: results span six datasets (D-NeRF, NeRF-DS, HyperNeRF, Nerfies, iPhone, and the 50-scene MonoDyGauBench), experiments are repeated three times and averaged, and detailed ablations cover group count J (Appendix A.3), soft/hard pruning ratios (A.4), and per-scene metrics (A.5). This substantially strengthens the empirical claims.

The three components are complementary and coherently integrated: TSP generalizes second-order/gradient-based pruning (PUP-3DGS, Speedy-Splat) to the temporal domain with a principled score (Eqs. 5–6); TSS is a simple but sensible timestamp perturbation that exposes temporally unstable 'floater' Gaussians; GroupFlow distills the learned deformation field into J shared SE(3) transforms via trajectory clustering and Umeyama alignment (Eqs. 8–11), reducing per-Gaussian MLP inference to per-group rigid motion.

Evidence is presented honestly: the paper explicitly reports the quality–speed tradeoffs (e.g., PSNR drops on D-NeRF for the full pipeline, 4DGS+GroupFlow falling below RTGS in PSNR), includes a limitations section, and discusses GroupFlow's regularizing effect in noisy scenes (Fig. 6, iPhone creeper).
Clear presentation: the method is well illustrated (Figs. 1, 2, 4), notation is consistent, and the relationship to prior pruning and motion-grouping work is accurately positioned.
weaknesses: Limited novelty in individual components: TSP is a direct temporal extension of existing gradient-based pruning (PUP-3DGS, Speedy-Splat), TSS is essentially a data augmentation on timestamps, and group-wise SE(3) motion modeling closely resembles prior motion-grouping methods (SC-GS, SPGaussian, DynMF, RiTGS). The contribution is primarily a well-executed combination and adaptation to deformable 3DGS rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Image quality does not fully survive the full pipeline in all settings: on D-NeRF the full configuration drops PSNR from 36.19 to 35.07 and degrades LPIPS (0.0172→0.0365) relative to the baseline; on 4DGS, pruning and GroupFlow each reduce PSNR (23.55→22.44→21.00), falling below RTGS. The claim of 'preserving neural-field fidelity' holds on NeRF-DS and HyperNeRF but is weaker elsewhere.

Several design choices are empirically fixed on the evaluated datasets (J=2048, λr=0.5, β=0.1, Nmax=100, 60%/30% pruning ratios), raising mild overfitting concerns; ablations mitigate this but the tuning protocol (tuned on the test datasets) is not discussed as a limitation.

Runtime comparisons have some fragility: baselines trained on A6000 for HyperNeRF due to memory, FPS measured on 3090 but training on A5000/A6000, and Figure 1 quotes numbers (438.86 FPS, 33.13×) that differ from the averaged table values (~505 FPS, 10.68×) without full reconciliation of which configuration/hardware each refers to.

Comparisons against recent efficient dynamic methods mentioned in related work (e.g., MEGA, LGS, Compact/Dash-based variants) are absent; the evaluation is restricted to applying the modules to DeformableGS and 4DGS backbones, so the effectiveness relative to natively efficient architectures remains partially unexplored.
No explicit code-release statement is made, which limits reproducibility given the many pipeline-specific hyperparameters and the custom MDGB wrapper noted in Appendix A.6.
